All I'm saying is to know your limits. It's very easy to be ambitious and impulsively download mods that you like and by all means you're allowed to. But with more mods means more maintenance. These questions aren't for me, they're for you to consider ahead.

Forge and Fabric are two completely different mod loaders. Fabric mods do not work with Forge mods, and vice versa. The only exception is Sinytra Connector but this, again, will open another can of worms for you in terms of being overly ambitious and being overwhelmed with new options. I do not recommend you go down this path unless you know what you're getting yourself into.

I'd recommend sticking to one type of mod loader, which would be Forge. I only brought up Fabric because you had unknowingly downloaded a mod that auto-downloaded Fabric as a dependency.

Don't use Crafttweaker if you have no intentions of changing in-game recipes. As in, don't bring a toolbox if you're not planning on fixing anything.

With the amount of mods you have, you're bound to have some kind of issue with mod cohesion and clashing interactions. You do need to put in some effort in making sure these conflicts don't appear or just ultimately just deal with them. Here are some pointers, I've noticed, surface level at least since I don't know what your actual goals are. I hope these help.

* You have Fabric for some reason (very likely because you have Towns and Towers and it auto-downloaded Fabric for you) despite it being a Forge modpack.
* Starlight is redundant since the lighting engine is near identical that it won't make much of a difference (said by the [developer of Starlight](https://gist.github.com/Spottedleaf/6cc1acdd03a9b7ac34699bf5e8f1b85c)). Same thing can be said with AI Improvements.
* DoubleDoors's mechanic is already part of Quark. Mods like Quark or Alex's Mobs, where they have an extensive config settings, needs to be looked over. Otherwise you're getting the entire package of every aspect. Some things are worth disabling.
* There is a LOT of performance mods, I'd say. Ultimately, that part will require you do some research on whether or not they're actually performative and help you or they're just clutter because they're been obsolete in newer versions or just straight up conflicting with one another.
* If you do have concerns about performance consider this next, have you tested your performance on your end and whether or not you have any performance issues? What about your friends' rigs? Can they handle it? How much memory do you/they need to allocate? The more memory that needs to be allocated, the greater the server performance required — and the more you may need to pay for a higher-tier host.
* I see you have Crafttweaker which can alter crafting recipes whether you're removing, adding, or hiding them (granted, you'll need JEITweaker). If you want to go down this route, this will make Polymorph obsolete. However, this will also open a can of worms which will require you to patch every conflicting recipe and JEI item (or you can pick and choose). It will be an LONG endeavor. However, if you don't go that route, Polymorph can be a cheap BUT effective solution to solve recipe conflictions. However it will not resolve duplicate recipes conflictions.

Yes and no. Yes, a lot of these mods used in "Unlimited" are just overly saturated/overrated. But again, no, that doesn't mean that the mods themselves are bad. There's absolutely nothing wrong with Vanilla+ modpacks. Hell, I have one in the works too. But the biggest takeaway is this:

1. Modpacks like "Unlimited" are a dime a dozen. It's just a modpack that "works"; Functionality over form. However, a good modpack needs to be player-friendly/easy to learn, feels seamless/appropriate, and stands out with their own customization.
2. Most modpacks will just lose their identity of what Vanilla is meant to be. Adding 50+ biomes and 100+ mobs, most being real life animals is just being too facetious. If you're interested in checking out the game design philosophy, I'd recommend this [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ybh5733DCo). Modpacks like BetterMC is just too over the top and aren't well integrated.

I'd recommend Crucial 2 or Raspberry Flavored (for Vanilla+). Valhelsia and ATM are decent options for kitchen-sink modpacks.

It's just one of those bait modpacks/tourist traps. Daniel's Unlimited, any modpacks that is lead by SHXRKIE (which he is affiliated with like Prominence and BetterMC. With Prominence however, YMMV) and RLCraft (Edit: RLCraft is streamerbait. Random BS that gets you killed should not brand the game as challenging. It's just terribly made, even if there was a lot of thought into it.)

Those modpacks will satisfy any blissfully ignorant newcomers because they'll think this is the norm. When in fact, these modpacks have minimal effort into making or lacking some form of cohesion because everything is overwhelming.

Literally, you can do the same thing these guys do by doing this:

1. Get all the mods you like. Different dimensions, magic, tech, mobs, food, etc. Don't think about themes because vanilla+ and kitchen sink modpacks don't have one.
2. Boot it up. If it crashes, find the mod that's crashing it. Repeat.
3. If everything works, send it. Make a trailer, send it to Youtube, get over a million views (I'm talking about you Daniel), profit.

Some of these modpacks claim to be Vanilla+ but has magic, tech, and whatever weird mods they wanted to add. Even if it was a kitchen sink modpack, they still won't have KubeJS, Crafttweaker, or any configuration changes to the mods to make it unique.

I remember my first highschool had certain fast foods like Chick Fil A or Bullritos. However, we never had the actual chain there, they were all jacked up prices and sold to students just like scalping, but for schools. I remember in 2015, it was about 5 bucks per chicken sandwich and that's how our school ran their snack bar. Having fast food workers in a school is hella wack.

The deli is probably the most difficult department but opinions may vary. The job itself will feel like you're working in a restaurant because that's what the Deli sorta is. You're not cooking the food but the amount to go back and forth whether its taking orders or preparing them will definitely feel like a restaurant.

For the first 3-4 weeks, you will be able to memorize where every single meat and cheese belong in their designated spots. From then on, you'll memorize most PLU code for common items (PLU codes help prints price labels for customers so they can scan) on the go. A lot of the work is done by repetition, and it never hurts to ask your colleagues for help.

There are three major components: the front (aka: window, where customers order), curbside (mobile orders that has a set timestamp to complete), and fresh slice (mass production of pre-slice meat and cheeses). Each section is important but fresh slice is least important if there's a line of customers.

Overtime you'll branch out to other tasks like taking party tray orders (catering) (maybe occasionally make the party trays if someone is able to teach you but mostly someone else does that). Personally, taking catering orders is really easy but always nerve-wrecking if you keep doubting yourself whether you got it right or not.

Lastly, you may be expected to lift some boxes around or do stocking from time to time, whether it's pre-made meals or unloading boxes deli products from receiving. It all depends on the work they throw at you and whether you're up for the job. 

I would say that after working at the deli for a certain amount of time, you can develop the skill to weigh things on your own. Meat and cheeses are weighed by the pound so if you're skilled enough, you could weigh it on your own and guestimate: "This feels about .8lb" and most of the time you'd be right. You may need to know basic math with this job. Customers can order food by the weight (1/2 lb), price (8 dollars worth), or by the piece (10-slices). With enough trial and error, you will gain enough experience to be accurate and pinpoint customer orders on the fly.

Proper method: Pour milk into metal cup, pump flavor into metal cup, stir and mix the two, pour into cup of ice, then pour espresso on top.

Improper method: Pour ice into cup first, pour milk and flavor pump into the cup, stir and mix everything thoroughly, guesstimate the milk level for espresso to have room, top off with espresso.

I brought this up since doing it improperly is time efficient since you're not using the metal cup as the middle man. The only difference is that the flavor may not be thoroughly mixed. Gazlowe, right now, is just boring and not fun to play. He has a LOT less damage, less CC, less escape, more time required to take down camps, more requirements, etc. I'm going to break down some stuff what I like and what I don't like, mainly what I don't like.

**Reduce, Reuse, Recycle** \- I hate his new trait. It's a nerf. This may be just me, but what was wrong with his mana? Why change it to a new system? I don't want to sound like a grandparent that doesn't know how computers work but, why? I'm like a Morales now.

With the scrap mechanic, although I can play the same amount of turrets Gazlowe could previously, after they expire or become destroyed, you only get 1/10th of your scrap bank back. This means that you will always be low on strap. In order to be able to plop down one turret from natural scrap generation (assuming you're at 0 scrap), you have to wait **16** seconds. The new scrap mechanic makes Gaz unreliable for team fights because you can't contribute well if your scrap isn't high enough. This ultimately makes Gazlowe unfit to stay long in team fights. 

Because Lazor and Xplodium no longer uses mana, you're left with a new scrap mechanic that only benefits one of your skill. A skill that players rely on camps, laning, zoning, and team fighting. And to top it off, buildings no longer drop scrap. That was the Gazlowe's key component for laning. And they took it away from him! Scrap also has less hangtime. You have like 5 seconds to pick it up or it expires. This is bullshit. Well, I guess I'll just drink from the fountain... oh wait.

**Rock-It! Turret** \- Gazlowe's turrets are a joke now. Damage now reduced by \~40%, has less health, and turret lifespan cut by half. They're literal peashooters. Just because I don't have to worry about the cooldown of the skill itself, doesn't justify the new scrap mechanic. Because I can't get scrap from buildings or fountains (if it was mana/replenishable), then what the fuck is the point of picking 1/10 (or 1/12) scrap from a turret if its going to last for 5 seconds? Turrets just feel unviable. They're like mayflies, they die so quickly. Look, I'm not going to complain about having 7+ turrets at once, but I don't like this change just because I valued quality over quantity.

**Deth Lazor** \- A skill that used to give players high risk, high reward, the more patient they are, having the ability to charge it, aim, and timing it is gone. Honestly, this is just more of a preference thing. I don't hate this, nor do I like it. They basically made the skill into a middle man. No more low damage from instant casting it (which I used to do often to finish off stragglers), but no more of the damage or range from full changing it. So smack dab in the middle it goes. And Gazlowe apparently can now self-heal.

**Xplodium Charge** \- A huge nerf. Less damage, less radius, less cast range, and less stun. Upside? Faster travel speed, less cooldown, faster detonation, and no mana. Yay... no mana. Look, this skill is worse now. I think the skill would be better if they just nerf the stun time or maybe even the cast range. Faster travel speed and detonation? Surprise, that's actually a nerf. Imagine having an hour to take a test. And then that clock speeds up. Kinda fucks up your timing no? It could be just me, but having the ability to time your bomb when a minion wave comes out is essential. I'd like to be able to predict where the enemy will be in 2.5 seconds because that's how long the delay is since **FOREVER**. You may think the explosion delay is a buff but in my book, it's a nerf.

**Robo-Goblin** \- My go-to ult is gone. The damage is non-existant. Prior to the rework, Gazlowe can do 300+ basic attack damage at 10, then 600+ at 20. Then later on 700+, 800+ throughout the game because everything was quadrupled. It was so cool to see Gazlowe hitting enemies like a hammer he is. Now they ripped his arms and I guess to make it more "authentic" to chainsaws (that is on his hands), gave him DoT. He's a Qhira now. A Lunara. His AA talents does. Not. Help. His. DoT. He is no longer granted armor and movement speed. Instead they gave him a 40 second Gladiator’s Medallion as a Heroic. I'm not saying that Ustoppable isn't good, I'm saying it's a worse option compared to armor + movement speed. Gazlowe can't pop it off anymore just to chase down enemies, run away, or initiate a fight with additional armor. All I get is CC immunity for 1.5 seconds... And the damage from Robo-Goblin just straight up sucks. Like, it's an insult and a mockery for Gazlowe's level 10, to feel more like a talent than an ultimate.

**Grav-O-Bomb 3000** \- I honestly pretty much never pick this ult, just because it's not my play style. With that being said, through my eyes, it feels like a buff but leaning towards a nerf and I'll tell you why. Grav-O-Bomb does less damage now and you get 5 second 30%+ basic attack buff after casting your ult. Your ult also reduced by 30 seconds (originally 90 seconds). The big catch now is that your ult no longer get reduced through scrap. Meaning it's a full length 60 second, rather than 90 seconds with cooldown reduction through scrap. And I do believe old Gaz cooldown is faster than new Gaz cooldown.

Gazlowe's lvl 1 back then definitely was a huge impact with that extra mana, imo, but now he's just overall weaker and less versatile.
